title: A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a manufactured or regenerated corneal replacement that restores a clear optical path through a scarred cornea containing abnormal blood vessels. It would replace or reconstruct opaque stroma—the cornea’s main structural layer—while maintaining a durable epithelial surface and enough mechanical strength for long-term function. The demanding target includes eyes with inflammation and limbal stem-cell deficiency, where the cells needed to maintain the corneal surface are depleted. Treatment would not require one human donor cornea for each recipient. This is a proposed combined capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement.

Successful integration would mean more than an initially transparent implant. The replacement would need to remain clear, structurally stable and covered by a healthy surface despite the recipient eye’s difficult biological environment. Stable nerve function belongs within this integration goal because corneal nerves support epithelial health, stromal integrity and wound healing. Preserving nerves during implantation and achieving durable functional reinnervation of a replacement are different accomplishments; the former does not establish the latter.

significance.text: A replacement meeting this target would combine visual rehabilitation in difficult scarred eyes with freedom from the requirement for an individual donor cornea. The 2022 Rafat study documents a substantial donor-cornea shortage and provides a technical basis for manufactured alternatives through collagen fabrication, storage and clinical implantation. The revolutionary step would be extending such manufacturing into durable optical and surface restoration in vascularized stromal scars, rather than demonstrating transparency or implantation alone.

The research supplied several estimates of the scale of need: 214,299 corneal transplants worldwide in 2022; a prevalence-based supply-demand ratio of approximately 1:55 when unilateral corneal vision impairment was included; and estimates attributed to Wang and colleagues of 5.5 million people with bilateral blindness or moderate-to-severe visual impairment from corneal opacity, plus 6.2 million with unilateral blindness. These numbers remain unverified in the supplied evidence: the JAMA article was not captured, and the retained Wang extraction contains only a redirect, without the reported EuropePMC passage. They therefore cannot serve as established quantitative premises here. The earlier 2.1 million estimate remains withdrawn. These limitations do not establish that the other estimates are false.

The direct benefit would be useful vision restored without allocating a whole human donor cornea to each treated eye. Wider access would be a conditional downstream possibility: affordable manufacturing, reliable distribution, appropriate surgery and sustained follow-up would still be necessary. Removing donor dependence addresses a major constraint but does not by itself create treatment infrastructure. The Rafat article explicitly recognizes that access also depends on economic, cultural, technological, political and ethical conditions.

Synthesis: this would be an advance in corneal repair, with benefits bounded by the rest of the visual system. Restoring the corneal optical path would not itself repair a damaged retina, reconnect an optic nerve or restore cortical visual processing. Likewise, success in scar-free keratoconus or in swelling caused by endothelial dysfunction cannot be assumed to predict success in vascularized stromal scarring.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is to achieve transparency, tissue stability and durable surface health together in a vascularized, scarred recipient bed. A material that remains clear in a relatively quiet cornea may behave differently in an inflamed eye with an unstable surface. The reviewed collagen work identifies long-term integration, stability and clinical outcomes as continuing questions and calls for investigation in stromal scarring. The target therefore requires evidence that clarity and structural integrity survive the recipient environment over time, rather than only evidence that a transparent implant can be manufactured.

Surface regeneration becomes a distinct barrier within the same replacement when usable limbal stem cells are absent. Holoclar shows that autologous epithelial reconstruction can address defined burn-related limbal deficiency, but its indication requires at least 1–2 mm² of undamaged limbus for biopsy. A replacement intended for eyes without that resource would need another durable means of maintaining its epithelial covering. Bilateral disease alone does not define this additional challenge, because Holoclar’s indication includes bilateral disease when sufficient undamaged autologous limbus remains.

Nerve integration is another part of this coupled problem. The reviewed article establishes the importance of sub-basal and stromal nerves for surface health, tissue integrity and healing, but the inspected nerve-preservation observations do not demonstrate durable reinnervation of the proposed replacement. A convincing solution would need to connect structural integration with sustained sensation and a healthy epithelial surface.

Engineering synthesis: the complete solution must also control recurrent vessel growth and immune injury, avoid progressive tissue weakening or surface breakdown, and permit consistent manufacture without consuming a whole donor cornea per eye. These are requirements of the proposed capability, not demonstrated properties of a particular product. The supplied evidence does not establish the original claim that rejection, glaucoma and surface breakdown constitute a verified pattern of penetrating-graft failure in this exact population; those outcomes should be assessed without treating that population-specific assertion as settled.

current_state.text: Rafat and colleagues, published online on 11 August 2022 in Nature Biotechnology, reported two uncontrolled pilot cohorts totaling 20 people with advanced keratoconus without corneal scars. Their cell-free porcine-collagen BPCDX implant was added without removing native corneal tissue. At 24 months, the corneas were thicker and flatter. Mean contact-lens-corrected visual acuity was 20/26 in the Indian cohort, while mean spectacle-corrected acuity was 20/58 in the Iranian cohort. The different correction methods matter: these values are not a uniform outcome measure across the cohorts. The study demonstrated an adjacent reshaping capability, not replacement of vascularized scar tissue or equivalence to donor transplantation.

Earlier collagen approaches extend beyond scar-free keratoconus. The supplement reviewed with the Rafat article summarizes clinical work involving superficial opacity and high-risk eyes, including a 2020 porcine-skin-collagen study of six patients with scarring, leukoma or dystrophies. That summary reports visual gains and one later stromal melt. It establishes relevant prior overlap and prevents a categorical assertion that manufactured collagen has never treated opacity. It does not establish the combined durable outcome proposed here in vascularized, inflamed eyes with limbal stem-cell deficiency, nor does the reported complication negate all benefit in the earlier patients.

EMA material documents European Union authorization of Holoclar, an autologous corneal epithelial-cell treatment, for adults with unilateral or bilateral limbal stem-cell deficiency caused by physical or chemical ocular burns. It requires a minimum of 1–2 mm² of undamaged limbus for biopsy and addresses corneal surface repair rather than replacement of opaque stroma. These conclusions are supported by the landing-page, overview and product-information passages described in the supplied review. That review had partial access to the relevant EMA material; it did not inspect the complete assessment dossier, and omitted sections cannot be assumed absent.

An Ophthalmology Breaking News editorial report dated 23 September 2026 attributes completion of US phase 3 ASTRA enrollment to an Aurion Biotech announcement. It describes AURN001 as cultured neltependocel combined with a ROCK inhibitor for corneal endothelial dysfunction and edema. Completion of enrollment is a trial milestone, not an efficacy result. Restoring endothelial pump function addresses fluid-related corneal clouding; this report supplies no demonstration of replacing established vascularized stromal scars.

The earlier research also attributed Japanese approval of neltependocel, marketed as Vyznova, in 2024 and a many-dose-per-donor manufacturing yield to Aurion-related reporting. The cited 25 September 2024 Eyewire item was not captured, and no PMDA decision document was supplied. Consequently, the approval date and donor-dose yield remain unverified in this record. That evidentiary gap does not establish that the reported approval or manufacturing claims are false.

The supplied evidence establishes these dated adjacent achievements but does not determine whether the complete vascularized stromal-opacity target remained unmet on 1 November 2026. No populated bounded search record was supplied to establish that contemporary boundary. The Rafat conclusions above rely on explicit article prose and eligibility criteria described in the review, rather than visual inspection of figures; some supplied PDFs also had incomplete text extraction. Those limits constrain additional interpretation without invalidating the reported 2022 clinical results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a manufactured or regenerated replacement would restore stromal clarity, a stable epithelial surface and prespecified functional visual acuity in eyes with vascularized stromal opacity for a prespecified multiyear period. The study should include a defined subgroup with bilateral limbal failure lacking a usable autologous limbal biopsy, while retaining stromal opacity as an eligibility requirement. Bilateral ocular-surface failure alone would not satisfy the target. The intervention must not require one human donor cornea per recipient. These are proposed criteria, not established clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Restore multiyear vision in vascularized scars including bilateral limbal failure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment: a prospective controlled study should permit comparison with penetrating keratoplasty where clinically appropriate, or with the relevant standard care for subgroups in which keratoplasty is not an appropriate comparator. Duration, functional-acuity thresholds, correction methods and acceptable complication rates should be specified before outcomes are assessed. Reporting should include vascularization, rejection, mechanical integrity, surface breakdown, corneal sensation, glaucoma, additional procedures and continuing treatment. The reviewed collagen article’s calls for controlled comparisons and longer-term investigation support this assessment approach, but do not prescribe these particular thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Compare outcomes against appropriate care using prespecified clinical criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: results should be reproduced across clinical centers and independently manufactured batches, with outcomes reported by baseline scarring, vascularization, inflammation and limbal function. Manufacturing consistency, storage and distribution requirements, surgical demands, follow-up burden and cost should be documented alongside clinical outcomes. A finite set of successful studies would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested populations, not universal suitability for every scarred or inflamed eye.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce clinical outcomes across centers and independently manufactured batches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: success confined to scar-free keratoconus reshaping, endothelial pump failure, or burn-related limbal deficiency with usable autologous limbus would remain valuable but would not complete OPH-04. A treatment addressing one layer could contribute to a combined replacement, provided the final demonstration establishes durable stromal clarity and surface integration in the intended vascularized scar population.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate durable stromal clarity and surface integration in vascularized scars

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPH-03, reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, shares the goal of restoring an optical path through an opaque anterior-eye structure. Its target is the lens, whereas OPH-04 concerns the corneal stroma and its surface. OPH-06, closed-loop control of axial eye growth, concerns eye length and refractive development. It remains distinct from both scar replacement and the corneal reshaping demonstrated in keratoconus.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-01, retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion-cell axons to brain targets, and OPH-10, arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, concern the neural pathway carrying visual signals. OPH-04’s nerve-integration goal concerns corneal sensation and tissue maintenance; it does not encompass optic-nerve reconnection or ganglion-cell protection. These capabilities could be complementary when corneal disease coexists with neural damage, but none substitutes for the others.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-02, biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE and their blood supply; OPH-07, programmable repair for multiple photoreceptor and RPE gene defects; and OPH-11, prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, all concern retinal function or preservation. OPH-04 restores the transparent entrance to that system. A clear cornea would allow light to reach the retina but would not establish retinal reconstruction, genetic correction or prevention of AMD progression.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-08, reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout, also involves blood vessels, but the therapeutic direction and tissue differ. It seeks restoration of retinal circulation, while OPH-04 seeks durable corneal clarity in an eye with abnormal corneal vascularization. Retinal reperfusion and control of corneal vessel ingrowth must therefore remain separate concepts.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-05, patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals, concerns generating visual information downstream of a failed ocular pathway. OPH-04 instead aims to restore an optical component of the natural pathway. OPH-09, reopening the human visual critical period, concerns visual-system plasticity; it might complement rehabilitation in selected patients after optical repair, but corneal clarity alone would not demonstrate renewed plasticity. No separate corneal-reinnervation entry is supplied in the roster, and nerve function remains part of OPH-04’s integration requirement.

change_log.change: Preserved OPH-04’s ID, title and central target while defining the achievement as combined stromal, epithelial, structural and nerve integration.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent innovation despite uncertainty about individual assertions and contemporary availability.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about collagen implants treating only keratoconus with a distinction between the 2022 scar-free additive procedure and earlier collagen work involving opacity and high-risk eyes.
change_log.reason: The reviewed supplement documents prior overlap, including a six-patient study with visual gains and one later stromal melt.

change_log.change: Expanded the 2022 results to include uncontrolled pilot design, 20 participants, absence of scars, retained native tissue, 24-month follow-up and different acuity-correction methods.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the quantitative achievement while limiting inappropriate comparison or extrapolation.

change_log.change: Corrected Holoclar’s scope to include adult unilateral and bilateral burn-related limbal deficiency and its 1–2 mm² undamaged-limbus biopsy requirement.
change_log.reason: Bilateral disease alone does not distinguish the proposed innovation from existing autologous surface repair.

change_log.change: Identified the September 2026 ASTRA source as an editorial news report attributing an announcement to Aurion, and separated enrollment completion from efficacy.
change_log.reason: The retained artifact is not the company release itself and does not establish a clinical outcome.

change_log.change: Retained the Japanese approval and many-dose-per-donor assertions only as unverified reports.
change_log.reason: The cited 2024 item was not captured, and a PMDA decision and manufacturing evidence were not supplied.

change_log.change: Qualified the worldwide transplant, supply-demand and visual-impairment estimates, while keeping the earlier 2.1 million figure withdrawn.
change_log.reason: The quantitative claims lack inspectable supporting content in the supplied record; missing evidence does not establish falsity.

change_log.change: Removed the unsupported population-specific graft-failure pattern as an established fact and retained relevant complications as proposed assessment outcomes.
change_log.reason: The review did not establish that rejection, glaucoma and surface breakdown describe the asserted failure pattern in this exact population.

change_log.change: Required vascularized stromal opacity in the proposed demonstration, including the bilateral limbal-failure subgroup, and added appropriate comparators, reproducibility and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original alternative eligibility route could have been met by surface repair alone; the revised criteria assess the intended combined capability without presenting a consensus standard.

change_log.change: Qualified broader access and present-day novelty, and mapped distinctions across all other supplied roster entries.
change_log.reason: Donor independence does not automatically provide affordable care, and the empty search record cannot establish the full target’s absence as of November 2026.

unresolved_issues: Whether any manufactured or regenerated replacement had achieved the combined target in vascularized stromal opacity by 1 November 2026 remains undetermined from the supplied record.

The reported 214,299 worldwide transplants, approximately 1:55 supply-demand ratio, 5.5 million bilateral blindness or moderate-to-severe visual-impairment estimate, and 6.2 million unilateral-blindness estimate require supporting article content and confirmation of population definitions.

The claimed 2024 Japanese approval date, exact approved indication and many-dose-per-donor yield for neltependocel/Vyznova remain unverified; the cited 2024 report and a PMDA decision were not supplied.

The long-term applicability of earlier collagen opacity studies to vascularized, inflamed eyes with limbal stem-cell deficiency is unresolved, including how baseline risk relates to reported stromal melt.
The optimal epithelial-cell source and durable nerve-integration strategy for eyes without usable autologous limbus are not established by these inputs.
Specific multiyear duration, functional-acuity thresholds, acceptable complications, subgroup comparators and ongoing-treatment limits remain to be defined for the proposed demonstration.

No substantive review recommendation was rejected. The unverified numerical estimates were preserved as explicitly qualified reports to retain the research’s quantitative detail, rather than omitted as the review’s proposed replacement text suggested.

brief.title: A replacement that clears a deeply scarred cornea
possible: People whose cornea—the clear front of the eye—has become scarred and invaded by abnormal blood vessels could regain useful vision without waiting for a whole donor cornea. A manufactured or regrown replacement would rebuild the cloudy structural layer and keep a healthy surface, even in inflamed eyes.
why: This would bring vision treatment to difficult scarred eyes while reducing dependence on scarce donated tissue. Manufacturing replacements could address a major barrier for patients who need a corneal transplant.

sources.showed: This is research on worldwide corneal transplant activity and the gap between supply and need.
sources.cited_for: It concerns the shortage that manufactured replacements would address.
sources.not_established: Transplant counts and supply estimates do not establish that a manufactured replacement works.

sources.showed: This is research estimating blindness and visual impairment caused by corneal clouding.
sources.cited_for: It concerns the burden of vision loss from cloudy corneas.
sources.not_established: Estimates of disease burden do not establish a treatment for scarred corneas.

sources.showed: Small uncontrolled pilot studies used implants made from pig collagen, a structural protein, to thicken and reshape corneas with keratoconus, a thinning disease. Vision improved, but participants had no corneal scars.
sources.quote: During 24 months of follow-up, no adverse event was observed.
sources.cited_for: Manufactured collagen can be implanted and improve vision in selected eyes.
sources.not_established: The studies did not establish lasting replacement of scars containing blood vessels or success in eyes lacking surface-renewing cells.

sources.showed: The agency describes Holoclar, a treatment that grows a patient's own cells to repair the corneal surface after burns. A study using past medical records found stable surfaces and improved symptoms and vision.
sources.quote: There were also reductions in patients’ symptoms, such as pain and inflammation, and improvements in vision.
sources.cited_for: Cells grown from a patient's remaining healthy tissue can restore a damaged corneal surface.
sources.not_established: Holoclar requires healthy tissue from the corneal edge and does not replace the cloudy structural layer beneath the surface.

sources.showed: This is a report about Vyznova, a cell treatment for disease of the cornea's inner fluid-regulating layer, and its launch in Japan.
sources.cited_for: It concerns a cell treatment for a different cause of corneal clouding.
sources.not_established: Treating the inner layer does not establish replacement of scar tissue containing abnormal blood vessels.

sources.showed: Aurion completed enrollment in a randomized trial of cells intended to restore the cornea's fluid-regulating inner layer. Treatment effectiveness remained unresolved.
sources.quote: The randomized study enrolled patients at 12 clinical sites in the United States.
sources.cited_for: Cell therapy for fluid-related corneal clouding has reached a large clinical trial.
sources.not_established: Enrollment establishes neither treatment effectiveness nor repair of established scars containing blood vessels.

shown: Rafat and colleagues have demonstrated manufactured implants that improve vision in scar-free corneas. Earlier collagen studies also reported gains in scarred eyes, alongside a case of tissue breakdown. These results do not establish lasting clarity, strength and surface health together in the intended difficult eyes.
missing: A replacement must stay clear and strong in scarred, inflamed eyes despite abnormal vessel growth and immune injury.
A healthy surface must last even when neither eye has usable stem cells, the cells that renew the corneal covering.
Nerves must reconnect and sustain sensation, surface health and healing.
Consistent manufacturing must support lasting clinical results without requiring a whole donor cornea for each recipient.

milestones.label: Useful vision lasting years in scarred eyes
milestones.explanation: A replacement without whole-donor dependence would have to sustain clarity, surface health and useful vision for years, including in people lacking usable surface stem cells in both eyes. This would demonstrate the combined capability.

milestones.label: Controlled comparisons with appropriate care
milestones.explanation: A controlled study would have to compare outcomes with appropriate care using advance criteria for vision, duration and complications. This would establish how benefits, harms and continuing treatment compare.

milestones.label: Repeatable outcomes across clinics and manufactured batches
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across clinics and separately manufactured batches, with outcomes by eye condition and practical demands documented. This would establish where treatment works and what delivering it requires.

milestones.label: Lasting clarity and surface health in vessel-filled scars
milestones.explanation: The final treatment would have to sustain a clear structural layer and healthy surface in scars containing abnormal vessels. Success in other corneal conditions alone would leave this target unmet.

uncertain: The best source of surface-renewing cells and the best way to achieve lasting nerve connections remain unresolved.
It remains unclear how earlier collagen results extend to inflamed, vessel-filled scars with depleted surface stem cells.
The required follow-up duration, useful-vision threshold and acceptable complication rates still need defining.

page.title: Bioengineered corneal replacement for vascularized stromal scars
page.definition: A bioengineered replacement restores transparency to vascularized stromal scars—opaque corneal connective tissue containing abnormal blood vessels—and maintains a renewing epithelial surface. Treatment works in eyes without usable autologous limbal stem cells, which replenish that surface, without allocating a whole human donor cornea to each recipient.

goal.need: The 2022 global survey compared annual corneal transplantation with prevalent corneal vision impairment. Its supply-to-need ratios describe population need, rather than waiting lists or confirmed surgical indications. Manufacturing replacements would remove the requirement to allocate a whole donor cornea to each treated eye.

figures.caption: Global corneal transplantation and prevalence-based need in 2022
figures.note: Activity data covered 122 countries representing 89.5% of the world population. The ratios use prevalent impairment, not transplant waiting lists.

statements.body: European Commission, Horizon 2020 ARREST BLINDNESS programme
statements.quote: bioengineered scaffolds to replace or regenerate the corneal stroma in cases of stromal thinning, scarring, dystrophy or trauma
statements.context: The programme objective also includes epithelial-cell delivery, neural regeneration and regression of corneal blood and lymphatic vessels.

completion.title: A bioengineered cornea restores transparency, vision and surface renewal without usable autologous limbus.
completion.criterion: A prospective clinical study demonstrates, in the same treated eyes at 12 months, opacity grade 0 (clear cornea with iris details visible), at least a one-line gain in corrected visual acuity, no or trace epithelial defects, and no or mild superficial vessels (confined to one quadrant, sparing the centre), without rescue corneal grafting. Recipients have vascularized stromal scars and bilateral limbal stem-cell deficiency without usable autologous limbus. Treatment uses no whole human donor cornea per recipient. The study meets its prespecified statistical success rule for this combined endpoint.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published stromal-replacement, ocular-surface and opacity-grading endpoints; no outside body was found setting this combined test.
completion.basis: Searches of regulator material, corneal-replacement standards, NEI and EU programmes, and registered stromal and epithelial trials found no test covering the complete combination. This synthesis joins the RHCIII–MPC visual endpoint, Holoclar surface criteria and the published opacity scale in the target population. Their combination is not externally validated. Twelve months is borrowed follow-up and does not establish multiyear performance.

milestones.title: A corneal scaffold supports epithelial cells and blocks vessels in alkali-burned rabbit corneas.
milestones.criterion: The scaffold is sterile, shows no cytotoxicity in cultured corneal epithelial cells, supports their growth and blocks vessel ingrowth after implantation in alkali-burned rabbits. The 2013 RHCIII–MPC protocol reports these preclinical results; implants without MPC and donor allografts developed vessel ingrowth. Its summary supplies neither rabbit sample size nor observation duration.
milestones.set_by: Filatov Institute, preclinical evaluations in Tables 1 and 2 of the NCT02277054 protocol; the tests and results are tabulated, without a universal acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: Bioengineered stromal implants cause no serious adverse reactions in an initial clinical study.
milestones.criterion: Assess the implanted replacement for serious reactions including marked redness, pain, adjacent-tissue swelling and anterior-chamber clouding. The 2018 open-label RHCIII–MPC study treated 7 high-risk eyes, with mean follow-up of 24 months. One patient developed fungal keratitis at 6 weeks and required donor keratoplasty; the investigators considered the infection unrelated to the implant. Burn-related eyes showed implant thinning or persistent vessels.
milestones.set_by: RHCIII–MPC clinical investigators, published primary safety endpoint in the seven-patient high-risk study.
milestones.threshold_quote: no serious adverse reactions such as excessive redness, pain or discomfort, swelling of adjacent corneal tissues or clouding of anterior chamber fluid.

milestones.title: A bioengineered stromal implant improves corrected visual acuity by at least one line over 12 months.
milestones.criterion: The RHCIII–MPC protocol specifies improvement of at least one corrected-acuity line in corneal opacity, with 12-month follow-up and baseline decimal acuity of 0.1 or worse. In the 2018 series, one infectious-scar patient improved from 1.6 to 0.1 logMAR by 6 months and maintained that acuity through 35 months; lower logMAR means better acuity. Separately, Rafat and colleagues reported 24-month improvement in 20 keratoconus recipients without scars on 11 August 2022; those results concern an adjacent indication.
milestones.set_by: Filatov Institute, NCT02277054 protocol, corneal-opacity efficacy endpoint; written for central ulcers or scars with surrounding clear stroma.
milestones.threshold_quote: improvement of 1 or more lines in

milestones.title: Cultured corneal epithelium achieves surface reconstruction in more than half of patients at 12 months.
milestones.criterion: At 12 months, success requires no or trace epithelial defects and no or mild superficial neovascularization: vessels occupy at most one quadrant without central involvement. The lower exact 95% confidence bound for the success proportion must exceed 50%. Holoclar achieved 75 successes among 104 analysed patients: 72.1%, 95% CI 62.5–80.5%. Its indication requires 1–2 mm² of undamaged autologous limbus. Separately, a 2024 study of allogeneic induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived epithelial sheets in 4 eyes reported no serious adverse events over 2 years; it did not replace stroma.
milestones.set_by: EMA, Holoclar assessment report, study HLSTM01; this criterion concerns epithelial reconstruction, principally after ocular burns.
milestones.threshold_quote: the lower bound of the 95% CI for the estimated proportion of successful transplantations was higher than 50%.

milestones.title: A bioengineered epithelium–stroma graft preserves the corneal surface for 24 months.
milestones.criterion: The graft maintains surface integrity without ulcer recurrence or detachment during the protocol's 24-month follow-up. In the NANOULCOR interim report published on 28 March 2023, 5 patients with 5 treated eyes had refractory trophic ulcers, stromal degradation or fibrosis, and limbal stem-cell deficiency. No ulcer relapse, detachment or reoperation occurred; 4 non-severe adverse reactions were recorded. Sustained opacity improvement occurred in 2 eyes. This establishes combined surface repair, while leaving the complete optical and recipient-population endpoint unresolved.
milestones.set_by: Andalusian Initiative for Advanced Therapies, NCT01765244 published protocol, ulcer recurrence and stromal-repair endpoints over 24 months; written for refractory trophic ulcers.
milestones.threshold_quote: ulcer persistency or relapse and corneal stromal repair

not_found: No externally defined completion test was found combining vascularized stromal replacement, epithelial renewal and absence of usable autologous limbus.
No published clinical result was found satisfying that complete combination under one prospectively defined endpoint.
The RHCIII–MPC protocol's rabbit summary does not give the animal sample size or follow-up duration.
No externally specified population success threshold was found for the combined completion endpoint.

results.detail: The study used a different implant and treated patients without corneal scarring; it did not assess the specified high-risk scar population.

results.finding: NANOULCOR recipients: all 5 eyes achieved ocular surface stabilization over 24 months.
results.detail: The report does not give a 12-month success count using the specified epithelial-defect and vessel criteria, or an exact confidence bound exceeding 50%.
results.quote: All five eyes treated with NANOULCOR achieved ocular surface stabilization, with no ulcer recurrence throughout follow up.

results.finding: RHCIII–MPC implants blocked vessel ingrowth in alkali-burned rabbits; sample size and duration not reported.
results.detail: The protocol reports sterile implants, no cytotoxicity and epithelial cell growth. Ingrowth occurred with implants without MPC and donor allografts. It says Filatov Institute experiments confirmed the vessel-ingrowth finding.

results.finding: RHCIII–MPC implants resisted vascular ingrowth and supported epithelial coverage in 4 alkali-burned rabbits.
results.detail: Implants were followed for nine months. The source does not report sterility or cytotoxicity and growth in cultured corneal epithelial cells; it also does not specify vascular ingrowth outcomes separately for the control groups.
results.quote: Notably, RHCIII-MPC implants exhibited resistance to vascular ingrowth while supporting endogenous cell and nerve repopulation.
